result.summary: Pausanias describes the Cnidians' building at Delphi, the Lounge, and the first of Polygnotus' paintings in it, showing the fall of Troy and the Greeks preparing to sail home. He identifies many figures, comparing them with Homer and the poet Lescheos.

scenes.title: The Lounge at Delphi
scenes.summary: Pausanias introduces the Cnidian building called the Lounge and cites Homer on such meeting places.

scenes.title: Menelaus' ship and camp
scenes.summary: The painting shows Menelaus' fleet preparing to sail, with Phrontis the pilot and men striking tents.

scenes.title: Helen and the wounded heroes
scenes.summary: Helen sits with her handmaids among wounded Greeks, while Æthra and Demophon are shown and Lescheos' story of her rescue is told.
scenes.stakes: Æthra, a captive, hopes to be freed from slavery.

scenes.title: Trojan women and Nestor
scenes.summary: The captive Trojan women, Andromache, Medesicaste and Polyxena, appear, followed by Nestor and a horse by the shore.
scenes.stakes: The Trojan women face captivity and death.

alias_notes.explanation: Delphians' name for the Cnidian building, from its use as a meeting place.

notable_quotes.reason: Homer's line shows that lounges were common social gathering places in Greece.

analysis.text: Pausanias reads the painting as a text, checking its figures against Homer and the cyclic poet Lescheos.
Polygnotus' Delphi paintings were famous classical works; Pausanias' detailed description is a main source for them.

fun_facts.text: Lescheos' Little Iliad is lost, so Pausanias preserves some of its content.

language_notes.text: "Lounge" translates the Greek leschē, a public place for idle talk and gatherings, which is why Pausanias explains the name.
Melantho, a maidservant in Ithaca, insults the disguised Odysseus in the Odyssey, telling him to go sleep at a smithy or a public lounge.
Punting poles are long poles used to push a boat along in shallow water.
In the Odyssey Nestor tells Telemachus that Menelaus' pilot Phrontis died off Sunium, which delayed Menelaus' return.
Lescheos of Pyrrha was the poet of the lost epic Little Iliad, here called his Capture of Ilium. Pausanias uses him to check Polygnotus' details.
Æthra was taken to Troy as Helen's slave after Helen was carried off from Athens by Theseus' sons' kin; her rescue is the story told here.
The Epigoni were the sons of the Seven against Thebes; Adrastus led the original expedition and founded the Nemean games.
The baby is Astyanax, Hector's son, whose death after Troy's fall is told in differing versions.

context_notes.text: Polygnotus of Thasos was a famous fifth-century BC painter. His murals at Delphi were celebrated, and Pausanias describes them in detail.
Briseis was Achilles' captive woman in the Iliad; Diomede here is a woman's name, not the hero Diomedes.
Helenus, a son of Priam, was a Trojan seer who later went over to the Greeks.
Æthra, mother of Theseus, was said to have been Helen's slave at Troy. Her grandson Demophon came to rescue her.
Nestor, the aged king of Pylos, was the Greeks' wise counselor at Troy.

literary_notes.text: Pausanias infers the painter's reading from the accuracy of the wounds, reasoning from evidence as a critic rather than simply reporting.
The women's posture shows their grief and foreknowledge of slavery, giving the painting emotional force through attitude rather than action.
The pebbles alone suggest the shore, a spare visual detail showing the painter's economy of setting.
